- `src/spec/resources/generated/python/petstore_client/value_serializer.py:102` — return quote(value, safe=";=,:@!$&'()*+")
- `src/spec/resources/generated/dart/lib/src/abstract_api_client.dart:167` — uri = Uri.parse(url);

Each value-serializer defect above survives because petstore has no parameter that exercises it. These additions would catch each one through existing echo or captured-request tests: (a) an exploded array query param (style form, explode default), for ruby's last-value collapse. (b) A wire assertion on the required `category` query value containing `& = + # / ? space é`, for the kotlin injection (and java/node safe-set drift). (c) An echo assertion on `revision` that uses the full reserved set including `+ [ ] '`, for ruby/python/dart/swift/node/rust transport rewrites. (d) Optional integer and boolean query/header params (e.g. `limit`, `X-Trace-Sample`), for go's pointer addresses. (e) `format: byte`, `format: time` and `type: number` query params. (f) A uniqueItems array query param. (g) A deepObject param with a $ref model, and an object-typed form query param. (h) A `content: application/json` query param. (i) An array-of-date query param and a date path param with `style: matrix`. (j) date-time, enum and number fields in the setPetPreferences form. (k) A path value `..` that must be rejected or sent identically. Today the only reserved-character test is unit-level (`encodeQueryAllowingReserved("v1.0/beta:rc1")`), and kotlin's query wire test checks `category=dog` only.

## F066 [medium] allowReserved output is re-encoded by the transport URL parser in 6 SDKs, so reserved characters are not literal on the wire
- Status: **fixed** (done via decision D78 in all SDKs (batches 5-6, branch parity/spec-expansion)) | Lens: L01-value-serializer | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False

`encode_query_allowing_reserved` produces the same string in all 12, but some transports rewrite the URL after that. I checked each parser on `?r=a:b/c?d[e]f@g!h$i&j=1&k'l(m)n*o+p,q;r~s`. python (urllib3 2.6 `parse_url`, used by `PoolManager.request`), dart (`Uri.parse` in abstract_api_client) and swift (`URL(string:)` on macOS) re-encode `[`/`]` to `%5B`/`%5D`. node (undici fetch, WHATWG URL) re-encodes `'` to `%27`, and rust's reqwest `Url::parse` uses the same WHATWG special-query set, so it does too. ruby (Faraday decode/re-encode, see the separate finding) re-encodes every reserved character. java (java.net.URI), kotlin (Ktor), csharp, go and elixir keep them literal. The only allowReserved wire value petstore tests is `v1.0/beta:rc1`, and only through unit tests of the encoder, never through the transport. So `[ ] '` (and in ruby, all of them) differ on the wire without any test noticing. In node and rust the WHATWG `'` rewrite is unavoidable once a URL object is built, so those two are arguably forced. python, dart and swift could avoid it: urllib3 `request_url` with a pre-encoded url, `Uri(query:)` with `Uri.encodeQueryComponent` disabled, or `URLComponents.percentEncodedQuery`. Add an echo-based PetApi test that sends `revision` with the full reserved set and asserts the received query.

## F067 [medium] application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies in php and ruby skip ObjectSerializer.stringify (date-time, enum and number fields go out in non-canonical form)
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L01-value-serializer | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: php, ruby

In ten SDKs, each form value goes through the canonical scalar stringify: java toFormValue, kotlin, csharp, python, node, dart, go and swift stringify, rust's JSON scalar, elixir stringify. php's `buildQuery($body, true)` uses `(string)$v` for scalars and `json_encode($v)` for everything else. A DateTime field becomes `{"date":"2024-01-15 10:00:00.000000","timezone_type":1,"timezone":"+00:00"}` and a BackedEnum becomes `"sold"` with JSON quotes. I confirmed both with php 8.5. A float 1.0 becomes `1`. php's api layer only fixes `format: date` fields (`ValueSerializer::formatDateOnly`). ruby's `URI.encode_www_form(body.compact)` calls `to_s`, so a Time becomes `2024-01-15 10:00:00 UTC`. The canonical value is `2024-01-15T10:00:00.000+00:00`. A nil element inside an array is also handled three ways: skipped by 9 SDKs, emitted as `tags=` by elixir (stringify(nil)), and as an empty pair (`tags=a&&n=x`) by ruby. Petstore's form fields are strings and dates only. Add a date-time, an enum and a number field to setPetPreferences.

## F068 [medium] content-based query params (`content: application/json`) skip the SDK serializer in 8 languages, giving different JSON bytes and error types
- Status: **open** | Lens: L01-value-serializer | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: go, csharp, php, python, node, ruby, rust, elixir, java, kotlin, swift, dart

For a query param declared with `content: application/json`, java, kotlin, swift and dart call the SDK ObjectSerializer. The other eight call a raw stdlib JSON encoder. go uses `json.Marshal` and discards the error. HTML escaping stays on, so `<` becomes `<`, which contradicts the AGENTS 'Resolved' note that go serializes with SetEscapeHTML(false). csharp uses `System.Text.Json.JsonSerializer.Serialize` with default options: `<` becomes `<`, `é` becomes `é`, and the SDK converters for dates, enums and duration are skipped. php uses `json_encode` with no flags: `/` becomes `\/` and `é` becomes `é`. I checked this with php 8.5. python uses `json.dumps`, which puts spaces after `:` and `,`, applies ensure_ascii, and raises TypeError on a pydantic model. node uses `JSON.stringify`, so a Date ends in `Z`, not the canonical `+00:00`. ruby uses `JSON.generate`. rust uses `serde_json::to_string(...).unwrap_or_default()`, so a failure sends an empty string. elixir uses `Jason.encode!`, which raises Jason.EncodeError, not SerializationError. For `{"q":"a/b<é"}` the 12 SDKs put at least five different byte strings on the wire. swift's ObjectSerializer also leaves JSONEncoder's default slash escaping (`\/`) in place. Fix by routing every queryContent value through the SDK ObjectSerializer.serialize. Petstore has no content query param, so add one.

Reviewer suspected this is forced: None. Every SDK has an ObjectSerializer.serialize that applies the canonical JSON settings.

- `src/main/resources/templates/php/api/api.mustache:248` — $queryParams['{{baseName}}'] = json_encode($options->{{paramName}});
- `src/main/resources/templates/python/api/api.mustache:254` — query_params['{{baseName}}'] = json.dumps(options.{{paramName}})
- `src/main/resources/templates/node/api/apis.mustache:250` — queryParams['{{baseName}}'] = JSON.stringify(options.{{paramName}});
- `src/main/resources/templates/rust/api/api.mustache:395` — serde_json::to_string(&opts.{{paramName}}).unwrap_or_default()
- `src/main/resources/templates/java/api/api.mustache:333` — queryParams.put("{{baseName}}", objectSerializer.serialize(options.{{paramName}}()));
- `AGENTS.md:261` — go serializes with HTML escaping OFF (json.Encoder + SetEscapeHTML(false))

## F069 [medium] format: byte parameters are never base64-encoded, and each SDK emits a different wrong form
- Status: **open** | Lens: L01-value-serializer | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, csharp, python, ruby, node, php, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir

OAS `type: string, format: byte` means base64 text, and model bodies already round-trip it as base64 in all 12 (R8-1). The parameter path has no base64 step anywhere, so a byte query, header or path param with the value bytes "hi" serializes as follows. java and kotlin: `String.valueOf(byte[])` / `ByteArray.toString()` gives `[B@6d06d69c`, an identity hash. csharp: `byte[]` is an `IList`, so the value is treated as an array: `104,105`, or `p=104&p=105` when exploded. dart: `Uint8List` is a `List`, giving `104,105`. go: `toStringSlice` reflects over `[]byte`, giving `104,105`. rust: serde gives `[104,105]`. python: `str(b'hi')` gives `b'hi'`. swift: `Data.description` gives `2 bytes`. ruby, php, elixir and node send the raw bytes as text (`hi`; node through `Buffer.toString()`). The canonical value is `aGk=`. Petstore has no byte parameter. Fix by giving stringify a byte branch that base64-encodes, put it before the IList/List/slice checks in csharp, dart and go, and add a `format: byte` header or query param to petstore.

Reviewer suspected this is forced: None. Every language has a stdlib base64 encoder, and each object serializer already base64-encodes byte fields in bodies.

Petstore only has scalar date params with simple/form style. Add a date-array query param and a date path param with `style: matrix`.

## F071 [medium] format: time param stringify: kotlin throws a java.time exception, php sends a full date-time, and the others disagree on sub-seconds
- Status: **open** | Lens: L01-value-serializer | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True

Kotlin maps `time` to `LocalTime`, but `stringify` has no LocalTime branch. LocalTime matches `is TemporalAccessor -> DATE_TIME_FORMATTER.format(value)` with pattern `yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSSxxx`, which throws `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException: Unsupported field: YearOfEra`. I reproduced that with the same pattern on JDK 22. That is a raw library exception, which the AGENTS error contract forbids. java has the explicit LocalTime branch that kotlin lacks. php maps `time` to `\DateTimeImmutable`, so stringify emits a full RFC3339 date-time. Among the rest, java (ISO_LOCAL_TIME), node (PlainTime.toString) and rust (NaiveTime serde) keep the fraction: `10:30:00.123`. csharp (`HH:mm:ss`), python (`timespec="seconds"`), ruby (`%H:%M:%S`) and elixir (`Time.truncate(:second)`) drop it: `10:30:00`. go, dart and swift take a string. No time param exists in petstore.

## F075 [medium] Bare type:number precision: python and node decode through IEEE doubles (AGENTS claims they preserve full precision); java emits exponent notation; node accepts any string
- Status: **fixed** (AGENTS.md / PARITY_TODO.md corrected against the code (round 9 doc pass)) | Lens: L02-object-serializer | Category: doc-truth | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: python, node, java, kotlin, csharp

AGENTS.md says five SDKs 'preserve full textual precision' for format:number, naming python (Decimal) and node (branded Decimal + JSON.rawJSON). In fact python parses bodies with plain json.loads (no parse_float=Decimal), so Pet.weightKg 12345678901234567890.123 becomes Decimal('1.2345678901234567E+19') and 12.30 becomes Decimal('12.3') before pydantic sees it; on encode JsonNumber widens to float again (emits 1e-7, 1.2345678901234567e19, 1000.0). node parses with JSON.parse and the Pet constructor does String(number): 12345678901234567890.123 -> "12345678901234567000", 0.0000001 -> "1e-7" which is then emitted raw as 1e-7; node also accepts ANY string for weightKg ("abc" is kept and re-sent as a quoted JSON string), python accepts quoted "12.5", while java/kotlin/csharp reject quoted decimals. java writes BigDecimal with toString (WRITE_BIGDECIMAL_AS_PLAIN off): input 0.0000001 round-trips as 1E-7 and 1E+3 as 1E+3 (verified jackson 2.19.4), whereas kotlin uses toPlainString (0.0000001, 1000) and csharp decimal emits 0.0000001/1000. Python's README also claims Decimal 'preserves exact decimal representation'. Either fix (python parse_float=Decimal; node JSON.parse reviver context.source; java WRITE_BIGDECIMAL_AS_PLAIN) or correct AGENTS/README to list python/node with the lossy set.

## F078 [medium] The 1000-deep JSON nesting cap is not uniform: php accepts at most 999, swift at most 512
- Status: **fixed** (done in php; still open for swift) | Lens: L02-object-serializer | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True

java (StreamReadConstraints), csharp (MaxDepth), and the byte-scan SDKs (kotlin, python, node, go, rust, ruby, dart, elixir) accept depth 1000 and reject 1001. php passes depth=1000 to json_decode, whose depth counts one level more: 1000 nested arrays fail with 'Maximum stack depth exceeded', 999 pass (verified php 8.5). ## F080 [medium] date-time decode resolves non-RFC3339 input against the host clock/timezone (csharp, ruby, node, dart, php) — host-dependent instants
- Status: **open** | Lens: L02-object-serializer | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: csharp, ruby, node, dart, php, python

Distinct from the closed 'date-time input strictness' item (which is about rejecting vs accepting): here the SAME wire value decodes to DIFFERENT instants depending on the machine. Verified: csharp DateTimeOffset.TryParse(…, DateTimeStyles.None) maps "2024-01-01T10:00:00" to the host offset (+11:00 on the test host), accepts "01/02/2024 10:00" (US month-first), "Jan 1 2024", and "10:00" (=today). ruby Time.parse maps offset-less and date-only to host local and "10:00" to today's date. node new Date("2024-01-01T10:00:00") is host-local (ECMAScript), date-only is UTC. dart DateTime.parse of offset-less is a local DateTime and is then emitted with the host offset. php model fields: Symfony DateTimeNormalizer falls back to `new DateTime($data)` when the RFC3339_EXTENDED default format fails, so "tomorrow", "now", "next monday", "@1700000000" are accepted (verified php 8.5 + Symfony source), offset-less uses php.ini date.timezone; also any RFC 3339 value WITHOUT a 3-digit fraction ("2024-01-01T10:00:00Z") only parses via that lenient fallback. python's container/top-level path uses dateutil.parser.parse (accepts free-form text) though it rejects naive results. java/kotlin/go/rust/elixir never consult the host zone. ## F081 [medium] format:byte base64 decode strictness differs on padding, whitespace, alphabet and trailing bits (php model fields not validated at all)
- Status: **fixed** (done via decision D58 in all SDKs (batches 5-6, branch parity/spec-expansion)) | Lens: L02-object-serializer | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: kotlin, php, java, csharp, node, go, dart, python, swift, elixir, ruby, rust

Verified per language with each SDK's actual decoder: UNPADDED 'dGVzdA' accepted by kotlin (java.util.Base64.getDecoder) and php (base64_decode strict); rejected by the other 10. Embedded SPACE 'dGVz dA==' accepted by java (Jackson MIME_NO_LINEFEEDS skips whitespace), csharp (.NET 9 STJ), php, node (decodeBase64 strips /\s+/); NEWLINE additionally accepted by go (encoding/json ignores \r\n); rejected by kotlin, python(bare path), ruby, dart, rust, swift, elixir. URL-SAFE alphabet '-_8=' accepted ONLY by dart (base64Decode accepts both alphabets, even '%3D' padding). NON-CANONICAL trailing bits 'dGVzdB==' accepted by java, kotlin, php, python, node, go, swift, elixir; rejected by csharp, ruby, dart, rust. php model byte fields (PetPassport::$thumbnail etc.) are plain strings never validated on deserialize, so even '!!!!' is accepted until getThumbnailAsBytes() is called. Note java vs kotlin (same JVM) disagree on both padding and whitespace. node's comment claims to match 'the strict decoders in ruby/php/python/elixir/go/rust', which is false for php, go and python model fields. Pick one rule (RFC 4648 §3.3: reject whitespace and non-alphabet, require padding, reject non-zero pad bits) and pin it with a shared test vector table.

- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L02-object-serializer | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True

## F084 [medium] Binary body sent with a selected application/json Content-Type (setPetAvatar) gives {}, raw bytes or a base64 string depending on language
- Status: **fixed** (done via decision D35 in all SDKs (batches 5-6, branch parity/spec-expansion)) | Lens: L03-request-assembly | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, go, kotlin, rust, swift, node, csharp, php, python, ruby, dart, elixir

setPetAvatar declares image/jpeg, image/png and application/json. Every SDK types its body as a binary stream or bytes, and every SDK accepts `application/json` as the selector, which passes the R7 declared-type check. The body ladder then disagrees:
- java: an InputStream is not byte[], so it goes to objectSerializer.serialize(). FAIL_ON_EMPTY_BEANS is disabled, so the body is `{}`.
- go: *os.File goes to serialize() and becomes `{}`.
- kotlin: the ladder checks `body is ByteArray` before the content type, so raw image bytes are sent labelled application/json.
- rust: Vec<u8> passes through unchanged ('already serialized'), so raw bytes are sent as JSON.
- swift: Data is Encodable, so JSONEncoder sends a base64 JSON string.
- node: the ObjectSerializer replacer sends Buffer as base64.
The same call puts three different payloads on the wire, and none of them is the spec's `{data: <base64>}` envelope. The go template comment admits that 'the caller must still supply a body the selected content-type accepts', but no SDK can, because the signature accepts only the binary type. Fix: either reject a JSON selector when the body is binary, with the same ArgumentError/IllegalArgument in all 12, or generate the envelope. Petstore test: setPetAvatar(…, requestContentType=application/json) must have the same outcome in all 12.

## F085 [medium] Binary return type with an absent response Content-Type behaves differently in the 12 SDKs; java's BaseApi contradicts its own transport, and rust silently returns empty bytes
- Status: **open** | Lens: L03-request-assembly | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, rust, go, swift, node, python, elixir, php, kotlin, csharp, ruby, dart

Case: a binary-returning operation (downloadPetDocument and similar) whose response has no Content-Type. java's transport treats an empty Content-Type as TEXT and does not base64-encode it (DefaultApiClient.isTextContentType returns true, citing the 'established cross-SDK convention'). java's BaseApi mirror isTextResponseContentType("") instead returns FALSE, and its comment says this 'mirror[s] the transport'. BaseApi then runs Base64.getDecoder().decode() on a body that was never encoded: it throws IllegalArgumentException for most text, and returns wrong bytes for text that happens to be valid base64. The other languages:
- Return the raw UTF-8 bytes: kotlin, csharp, ruby. dart tries base64 first and falls back to UTF-8, so a base64-looking body is mis-decoded.
- Treat a missing Content-Type as JSON and fail on a raw body: go, swift, node, python, elixir, php.
- rust treats it as JSON, gets a parse error, and silently returns an EMPTY Vec<u8> with Ok (`_ => Vec::new()`). That is data loss with no error.
The same input therefore gives three different outcomes: bytes, an error, or silently empty. Fix: use one rule in every language. Recommended: a missing Content-Type on a binary return type means the transport kept the body as text, so return its UTF-8 bytes. java's mirror must match its own transport, and rust must not swallow the error. Petstore extension: a chasm route for downloadPetDocument that omits Content-Type, plus a unit test per language.

Reviewer suspected this is forced: None. This is an internal mirror bug in java plus an unharmonized policy.

- `src/spec/resources/generated/java/src/main/java/com/example/petstore/DefaultApiClient.java:767` — return true;

## F086 [medium] Percent-encoding safe set for normal query values and form bodies is not harmonized (~ * ! ' ( )); the R8-10 fix was applied to OAuth only
- Status: **fixed** (done via decision D52 in all SDKs (batches 5-6, branch parity/spec-expansion)) | Lens: L03-request-assembly | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, node, ruby, kotlin, csharp, php, python, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir

R8-10 fixed this exact class (keep only `-._~` literal, %-encode `* ! ' ( )`) in the OAuth token body, the Basic header and the authorize URL. BaseApi's general query and form encoders were not changed. Query values today:
- csharp (Uri.EscapeDataString), php (rawurlencode), python (quote, safe=''), ruby (CGI.escape), dart (Uri.encodeQueryComponent), go (url.QueryEscape), rust (urlencoding::encode), swift (explicit `-._~` set) and elixir (URI.encode_www_form) all emit `~` literal and `%2A%21%27%28%29`.
- java (URLEncoder plus `+`→%20) emits `*` literal and `~`→`%7E`.
- node (encodeURIComponent) emits `! ' ( ) * ~` literal.
- kotlin leaves everything literal (separate critical finding).
Form bodies split along a different line: java (URLEncoder), node (URLSearchParams) and ruby (URI.encode_www_form) use the WHATWG form set (`*` literal, `~`→%7E). csharp, php, python, dart, go, rust, swift and elixir use the RFC 3986 set (`~` literal, `*`→%2A).
I checked these with ruby 2.6, elixir, python3 and node: `a~b*c!d'e(f)g` gives ruby CGI `a~b%2Ac%21d%27e%28f%29g`, ruby www_form `a%7Eb*c%21d%27e%28f%29g`, node encodeURIComponent `a~b*c!d'e(f)g`, node URLSearchParams `a%7Eb*c%21…`, and python/elixir `a~b%2Ac%21d%27e%28f%29g`. A spec-compliant server decodes all of these to the same value, but the bytes on the wire differ and no test pins them. Fix: route query and form encoding through one shared per-language encoder with the rust unreserved set `-._~`, as R8-10 did for OAuth. Unit test: each BaseApiTest asserts that `a~b*c!d'e(f)g` gives `a~b%2Ac%21d%27e%28f%29g` in a query value and in a form value.

Reviewer suspected this is forced: None. Each language can use a hand-rolled unreserved encoder, as rust/dart/kotlin already do for RFC 5987 and OAuth.

## F087 [medium] Query, form-body and multipart part ORDER differs across SDKs; go, swift and rust multipart are nondeterministic per run
- Status: **open** | Lens: L03-request-assembly | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, go, swift, elixir, rust, python

The order of query parameters, form-urlencoded pairs and multipart parts is not the spec declaration order everywhere. Kotlin (LinkedHashMap), csharp, php, ruby, node, dart and rust (query and form use a Vec) emit declaration order. The others differ:
- java builds queryParams and formBody as `new HashMap<>()`. setPetPreferences sends `note…&nickname…&renewalDate…&tags…`, getPetTag sends `filter&sizes&colors&revision`, findPetsByStatus sends `filter[color]&filter[size]&bornAfter&status`, and the uploadPetDocument parts go in the order `file, notes, documentType`. I computed these with Java's HashMap.
- go ranges over `map[string]any` for the query string and multipart parts, so the order is random on every call. The form body goes through `url.Values.Encode()`, which sorts keys: `nickname&note&renewalDate&tags`.
- swift iterates `[String: Any]` Dictionaries for query, form and multipart. Swift seeds hashing randomly per process, so the order varies between runs.
- elixir builds query_params and request_body as maps. Maps of up to 32 keys iterate sorted, so `bornAfter&filter[...]&status` and multipart `documentType, file, notes`.
- rust multipart is `HashMap<String, MultipartValue>` with RandomState.
- python moves every allowReserved query param after all normal ones (normalized and reserved groups).
Wire bytes therefore differ between SDKs, and for go, swift and rust multipart they differ between runs. That breaks byte-level request recording, signature schemes that do not canonicalise, cache keys, and the governing rule of the same bytes on the wire. No test catches it: every multi-field assertion uses contains/split. The kotlin exact `nickname=a+b&tags=x&tags=y` and go `nickname=a+b&tags=x&tags=y` assertions only pass because those two keys happen to sort in declaration order. Fix: use ordered containers. Java: LinkedHashMap in api.mustache. Go: a slice of pairs, with no url.Values.Encode. Swift: KeyValuePairs or an array of tuples. Elixir: a keyword list or list of tuples. Rust: Vec for multipart. Python: keep one ordered pass. Petstore test: assert the exact full string for getPetTag with all four query params, setPetPreferences with all four fields, and the uploadPetDocument part order, in all 12.

Reviewer suspected this is forced: None. Every language has an ordered container: LinkedHashMap, slices of pairs, KeyValuePairs, keyword lists, Vec.

## F090 [medium] Environment proxy variables (HTTP(S)_PROXY/NO_PROXY) are honoured by some SDKs and ignored by others

When TransportOptions.proxy is null, ruby (Faraday reads proxy env unless ignore_env_proxy), php (Symfony HttpClient defaults to http_proxy/https_proxy/no_proxy), csharp (HttpClientHandler UseProxy=true with HttpClient.DefaultProxy reading env on Linux), rust (reqwest system/env proxy on by default; there is no .no_proxy()) and swift (system/libcurl proxy) route through an environment proxy. java (HttpClient), kotlin (Ktor CIO), python (urllib3 PoolManager), node (undici fetch), go (a bare &http.Transport{} without ProxyFromEnvironment) and dart (dart:io default findProxy) connect directly. - Status: **open** | Lens: L04-transport | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False

Proxy-Authorization authenticates to the configured proxy, which is the same proxy for every hop. java/kotlin/swift/dart inject it as a normal request header (proxyAuthHeader) and also list 'proxy-authorization' in the cross-origin strip set, so the redirected request through the proxy carries no proxy credentials. python deliberately deletes it from the ProxyManager's proxy_headers for the rest of the chain ('Guard 3'). dart-io can recover through addProxyCredentials challenge handling; the others get 407. csharp (WebProxy.Credentials), ruby (Faraday proxy user), php (Symfony proxy option), go (Transport.Proxy userinfo), rust (reqwest Proxy), node (ProxyAgent) and elixir (Mint proxy_headers) keep authenticating every hop. Testing needs the squid fixture with auth plus a cross-origin redirect.

Reviewer suspected this is forced: None. Re-add the transport's own proxy header after the strip (the strip should only remove caller-supplied credentials).

## F099 [medium] An ApiError for a response that arrived but could not be decoded has null headers in 6 SDKs and the real headers in 6, contradicting the documented null-headers signal
- Status: **open** | Lens: L05-errors | Category: error-contract | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, csharp, node, swift, elixir, php, python, ruby, dart, go, rust

AGENTS.md ('responseHeaders null vs empty is a signal') says null headers mean that no HTTP response arrived, and that null is reachable only through the transport-failure constructor. The decompression-failure error contradicts this. A response did arrive, and the error carries its real status, but java, kotlin, csharp, node, swift and elixir build it with null headers. java and kotlin use the ApiException(int, String, Throwable) constructor, which hard-codes responseHeaders = null. php, python, ruby, dart, go and rust attach the response's real headers to the same failure. A caller reading headers == null as 'no response arrived' gets the wrong answer in 6 SDKs. The two groups also disagree on whether, for example, x-request-id is available on this error. The same split appears on the redirect-limit error: java and kotlin pass null, python passes the real headers, and php passes the empty array [], because ApiException::__construct defaults $responseHeaders = []. The php default, plus node's ClientError and leaf constructors defaulting responseHeaders to {}, also means a php ApiException built without headers signals 'a response arrived with no headers'. Pick one rule, most likely the real headers whenever a status is known, and apply it in all 12. The java/kotlin/csharp (status, message, cause) constructor needs a headers parameter.

## F101 [medium] The typed-error-body accessor's failure contract differs: go returns a non-SDK error, node throws on an empty body, dart swallows every failure
- Status: **fixed** (done in dart; still open for go, node) | Lens: L05-errors | Category: error-contract | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: go, node, dart

In java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, swift and elixir, getTypedErrorBody returns null/None/nil for an absent or empty body and raises the SDK SerializationError for a malformed body, because all of them route through ObjectSerializer.deserialize. Three SDKs deviate. (1) go: GetTypedErrorBody calls the package-local unmarshalErrorBody, which returns a raw *json.SyntaxError or *json.UnmarshalTypeError, or a plain fmt.Errorf when the depth cap trips. It never returns *SerializationError, so errors.As(err, new(*SerializationError)) fails, which breaks the 'SerializationError for every encode/decode failure' contract. It also skips the BOM strip that go's own deserialize does. (2) node: getTypedErrorBody treats only null as absent. An empty-string body goes to ObjectSerializer.parseJson(""), and JSON.parse('') throws SerializationError, where every other SDK returns null for "". (3) dart: the accessor catches every exception and returns null, including malformed JSON, a type mismatch and a JSON array body (the `as Map<String, dynamic>` cast), so a decode failure is indistinguishable from 'no body'. The go test only checks that an error is non-nil, never its type, and no node test covers an empty-string body.

R5-3 aligned rust's success path to the 1000-deep cap: object_serializer::deserialize does a byte-scan, calls disable_recursion_limit and strips the BOM. Fix: route both helpers through crate::object_serializer::deserialize::<T>(bytes). This is what java, kotlin, python, ruby, node, dart, swift and elixir do for the error path.

## F105 [medium] swift ApiError.fromResponse drops a scalar JSON error body (JSONSerialization without .fragmentsAllowed)
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L05-errors | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: swift

swift's fromResponse calls JSONSerialization.jsonObject(with: data) with no options, which rejects a top-level fragment. An error body of `"Not found"`, `123` or `true` therefore leaves errorBody nil in swift. The other 11 parsers accept top-level scalars: java Jackson Object.class, kotlin parseToJsonElement, csharp JsonDocument.Parse, php json_decode, python json.loads, ruby JSON.parse, node JSON.parse, dart jsonDecode, go json.Unmarshal into any, rust serde_json::Value and elixir Jason. All of them populate errorBody with the scalar. I confirmed this with a swift script on this host: each of the four fragment inputs threw, and only `{"a":1}` parsed. ## F106 [medium] ApiKey/Basic/Bearer unit-test coverage differs by language, and no SDK tests non-ASCII (UTF-8) Basic credentials
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L06-simple-auth | Category: test-gap | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: dart, node, java, ruby, php, elixir, kotlin, csharp, python, go, rust, swift

Missing cases by language. dart Bearer: no prefix-dedup test at all (already-prefixed, lowercase, mixed-case). dart ApiKey: no empty or whitespace rejection test, no CR/LF/NUL test for query or cookie, no cookie-location test; its test 'non-header locations accept arbitrary chars' is misleading, because CR/LF/NUL are rejected at every location. node ApiKey: no cookie-location test and no CR/LF/NUL query or cookie test. node Bearer: no mixed-case dedup test. java Bearer: no CR/LF or non-ASCII rejection test. java ApiKey: no cookie happy path, no header non-ASCII rejection, no query-accepts-non-ASCII test. Most suites assert `throws` or a substring instead of the exact message for every branch, which is how the java order divergence and the go/rust wording drift went unnoticed. No language has a Basic test with non-ASCII credentials: all fixtures use 'alice:s3cret' or 'user:pass'. Nine SDKs transcode to UTF-8 by construction. php, elixir and ruby base64 the raw string bytes, and ruby strings carry their own encoding: an ISO-8859-1 `"café"` yields Latin-1 bytes (`Y2Fm6Q==` instead of `Y2Fmw6k=`), and mixing UTF-8 and Latin-1 parts raises Encoding::CompatibilityError. Fix: add a shared table to every language's Basic test, e.g. `('ünïcødé','pässwörd') -> Basic w7xuw69jw7hkw6k6cMOkc3N3w7ZyZA==`. Consider `.encode(Encoding::UTF_8)` in ruby.

## F108 [medium] go authenticators leak secrets through %#v because they implement Stringer but not GoStringer
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L06-simple-auth | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: go

go redacts by giving `*ApiKeyAuthenticator`, `*BasicAuthenticator` and `*BearerAuthenticator` a `String()` method. `fmt` ignores `String()` for the `%#v` verb and prints every struct field by reflection, unexported ones included. So `fmt.Sprintf("%#v", auth)` gives `&auth.BearerAuthenticator{..., token:"super-secret"}`. The same happens for the per-scheme wrappers, which embed the base pointer, and for `%v` on a dereferenced value, because `String` has a pointer receiver. `%#v` is a common debugging and test-failure verb. The other SDKs' standard debug formatters (rust `{:?}`, python repr, ruby inspect, node util.inspect, java/kotlin/csharp/dart toString) are all redacted. The go test checks only `String()`, `%v` and `%+v`. Fix: add a `GoString()` method that returns the redacted form. OAuth authenticators (client_secret, refresh token) have the same gap. Unit test: add `%#v` to the format list in go/test/*_authenticator_test.go RedactsSecret.

## F109 [medium] java checks API-key and Bearer input in a different order, so a newline-only or control-only value gets a different error message than in the other 11
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L06-simple-auth | Category: message | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java

The other 11 SDKs check 'empty/whitespace-only' first, then CR/LF/NUL (ApiKey) or printable ASCII (Bearer). java folds both into one character loop that throws on the first bad character, and only decides 'all whitespace' after the loop. Concrete cases: ApiKey (any location) "\n" or "\r\n" gives java `API key value for 'X' contains forbidden control characters (CR/LF/NUL)`, while kotlin/csharp/php/python/ruby/node/go/dart/rust/swift/elixir give `API key value for 'X' must not be empty`. Bearer "\n", "\x0b" or "\r\n" gives java `Bearer token must contain only printable ASCII characters (RFC 7230 §3.2.6)`, while the other 11 give `Bearer token must not be empty`. A blank line read from an env file is a realistic input. The kotlin template on the same JVM checks `isBlank()` first, so the order is not forced. Fix: run the whitespace-only check before the character loop, as in kotlin. Unit tests: ApiKeyAuthenticatorTest and BearerAuthenticatorTest in all 12 should assert the exact message for "\n" and "\r\n".

## F110 [medium] php authenticator constructors do not mark secret parameters #[\SensitiveParameter], so secrets appear in exception stack traces (the docblock claims they do not)
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L06-simple-auth | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: php

`__debugInfo` masks secrets for var_dump and print_r, and the docblock says the class is safe for 'stack traces / error logs'. That is not true for traces. PHP records call arguments in exception backtraces whenever `zend.exception_ignore_args` is Off. Off is the built-in default and the php.ini-development setting, and official Docker images ship without a php.ini. So when validation in `BearerAuthenticator::__construct($host, $token)` throws, the token (truncated to 15 bytes) appears in `getTraceAsString()`. The per-scheme wrappers forward the secret through `parent::__construct`, so it can appear twice. composer requires php ^8.5, where `#[\SensitiveParameter]` is available, but no file in the SDK uses it. `var_export()` also bypasses `__debugInfo`. No other SDK puts call arguments into its error traces. Fix: mark `$token`, `$apiKey`, `$password` (and the OAuth `$clientSecret` and `$password` parameters), including the wrapper constructors, with `#[\SensitiveParameter]`. Unit test: in php/tests/BearerAuthenticatorTest.php, set `ini_set('zend.exception_ignore_args','0')`, construct with an invalid secret, and assert that `getTraceAsString()` does not contain it.

## F111 [medium] swift authenticators leak secrets through dump()/Mirror because they redact description but have no customMirror
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L06-simple-auth | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: swift

Swift redacts only `description` and `debugDescription`. Swift's standard `dump(_:)` and `Mirror(reflecting:)` walk the stored properties, private ones included. I checked this with a local swift script that copies the generated pattern: `dump(BearerAuthenticator(...))` prints `- token: "super-secret"` under the redacted header line. php handles its equivalent debug dump (`var_dump`) explicitly with `__debugInfo`, but swift does not handle `dump`. Fix: conform ApiKey/Basic/Bearer (and the OAuth authenticators) to `CustomReflectable` with a mirror whose secret children are `"***"`. Unit test: in BearerAuthenticatorTests.redactsSecret, capture `dump(auth, to: &out)` and assert the token is absent.

## F113 [medium] OIDC authenticator never requests the `openid` scope
- Status: **open** | Lens: L07-oauth-oidc | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir

Uniform gap. Every SsoAuthAuthenticator wrapper passes empty scopes (listOf()/[]/nil/vec![]), and OpenIdConnectAuthenticator adds nothing, so the authorize URL has no scope parameter. OIDC Core §3.1.2.1 requires scope to contain 'openid'; without it the request is plain OAuth2 (no id_token) and OPs such as Google reject a missing scope. ## F114 [medium] RFC 6749 §5.2 error parsing: go loses `error` when error_description/error_uri is non-string; kotlin stringifies numeric `error` and loses it on object/array description

## F116 [medium] Unclamped expires_in / discovery max-age arithmetic: swift traps, rust panics, java/csharp/ruby throw raw runtime exceptions, kotlin/go silently wrap
- Status: **partial** (done in rust; still open for csharp, dart, go, java, kotlin, ruby, swift) | Lens: L07-oauth-oidc | Category: error-contract | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: swift, rust, java, csharp, ruby, kotlin, go, dart

A server-supplied huge/infinite lifetime is not clamped before date arithmetic. swift: Int(d.rounded(.down)) traps the process for expires_in > Int.max (e.g. 1e20, verified with a probe: 'Double value cannot be converted to Int'). rust: f64→u64 saturates, then Instant::now() + Duration::from_secs(u64::MAX-30) panics ('overflow when adding duration to instant'); same for OIDC max-age. java: textual branch of parseExpiresIn has no NaN/Infinity guard, so "Infinity"/"1e400"/1e20 become Long.MAX_VALUE and Instant.plusSeconds throws ArithmeticException: long overflow (probed); values > ~3.1e16 throw DateTimeException; OIDC max-age likewise. csharp: DateTimeOffset.AddSeconds throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for ~2.5e11..9.2e18. ruby: Float("1e400").floor raises FloatDomainError (not rescued; probed). kotlin: (expiresIn-30)*1000 overflows → expiry in the past → refetch on every call; go: time.Duration(n)*time.Second overflows for > ~9.2e9 s. dart: Duration/DateTime.add range (unverified). python/node/php/elixir cache normally. These escape as non-SDK exceptions (or a crash) instead of the OAuth2TokenError/'stale' contract every other edge case follows. Fix: clamp expires_in and max-age to a sane ceiling (e.g. 1 year) in all 12 and add a unit row for 1e20 and "Infinity".

## F117 [medium] csharp normalizes redirect_uri through System.Uri.ToString() (trailing slash, default port, host case, unescaping) — bytes differ from the configured value
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L07-oauth-oidc | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: csharp

csharp types redirectUri as System.Uri and emits `_redirectUri.ToString()` in both the authorize URL and the code-exchange body. Uri.ToString() returns the canonical unescaped form: a host-only redirect 'http://localhost:8080' becomes 'http://localhost:8080/', ':443' is dropped, the host is lower-cased, and percent-escapes are unescaped before EscapeDataString re-escapes them. OPs compare redirect_uri by exact string (RFC 6749 §3.1.2.3), so csharp can fail with redirect_uri_mismatch where the other 11 send the string verbatim. R8-F2 only covers the OIDC endpoint being a Uri. Use OriginalString (or keep redirect_uri a string). PLAUSIBLE: .NET behaviour stated from documentation, not executed here.

## F118 [medium] elixir auth-code/OIDC: exchange_code returns a new struct the Client never sees, so API calls keep raising 'Must call exchange_code'
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L07-oauth-oidc | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: elixir

In the other 11, exchangeCode on the authenticator instance the client holds completes the flow. In elixir, OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator.exchange_code returns `%{self | token_exchanged: true}` — the flag lives in the struct, not in the shared token-manager Agent — and Client.new stores its own copy, so every API call through the Client raises 'Must call exchange_code before making API requests'. For OIDC, set_api_client returns `%{self | api_client: client}` only on the Client's copy, so calling exchange_code/build_authorization_url on the user's struct hits the `api_client: nil` clause and raises 'ApiClient has not been injected'. The elixir tests only exercise these by calling set_api_client manually and auth_headers directly, never through Client.new. Not forced: the SDK already shares mutable state via Agents (token manager, discovery_cache); the exchanged flag/api_client should live there too.

## F119 [medium] exchangeCode() is silently ignored when a token is cached or a refresh token exists (goes through the caching getAccessToken)
- Status: **fixed** (done via decision D03 in all SDKs (batches 5-6, branch parity/spec-expansion)) | Lens: L07-oauth-oidc | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir

Uniform defect. exchangeCode/exchange_code calls tokenManager.getAccessToken(tokenUrl, codeParams), which first returns any still-valid cached token, and otherwise tries the refresh_token grant (and returns its result on success) before ever POSTing grant_type=authorization_code. A second exchangeCode (user re-login / account switch / scope upgrade on a long-lived authenticator, or OIDC) therefore never sends the new code: the old identity's token keeps being used and tokenExchanged is set to true. The code exchange should bypass the cache and refresh path (direct fetch, replacing access/refresh tokens).

## F121 [medium] A zero or negative timeout means something different in each SDK; only rust validates it
- Status: **open** | Lens: L08-config | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir

Every builder takes the timeout with no range check except rust, whose build() returns ConfigurationError::InvalidTimeout for a negative value. The other 11 pass the raw number to their HTTP library, giving library-specific results (from library semantics, not run here). java: Duration.ofMillis(<=0) passed to HttpClient.Builder.connectTimeout and HttpRequest timeout throws a raw IllegalArgumentException at client construction or request time. kotlin: Ktor HttpTimeout requires values > 0, raw IAE. csharp: HttpClient.Timeout throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for 0, but -1 equals Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan, so timeout(-1) silently means no timeout. python: urllib3.Timeout(total<=0) raises ValueError on every request rather than at configuration. node: AbortSignal.timeout(-1) throws RangeError per request (verified locally), and 0 aborts immediately, giving NetworkTimeoutError. go: http.Client sets a deadline only when Timeout > 0, so 0 and negative both mean no timeout. rust: 0 is a zero deadline (immediate timeout), negative is rejected at build. php: max_duration=0 is Symfony's 'unlimited'. dart: Future.timeout with a negative duration fires immediately. Same input, different accept/reject and wire outcome. Under the error contract a negative timeout is a caller mistake and should be rejected at configuration, as rust does. A shared rule (reject < 0, decide whether 0 means no deadline) is needed.
- `src/spec/resources/generated/rust/src/transport_options.rs` — if ms < 0 { return Err(ConfigurationError::InvalidTimeout(ms)); }
- `src/spec/resources/generated/java/src/main/java/com/example/petstore/TransportOptions.java:264` — public Builder timeout(@Nullable Integer timeout) { this.timeout = timeout; return this; }
- `src/spec/resources/generated/go/pkg/default_api_client.go:299` — client.Timeout = time.Duration(*opts.Timeout()) * time.Millisecond
- `src/spec/resources/generated/csharp/src/PetstoreClient/DefaultApiClient.cs:244` — _httpClient.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(transportOptions.Timeout.Value);
- `src/spec/resources/generated/node/src/abstract-api-client.ts:296` — fetchOptions.signal = AbortSignal.timeout(this.transportOptions.timeout);
- `src/spec/resources/generated/python/petstore_client/default_api_client.py:415` — request_kwargs["timeout"] = urllib3.Timeout(total=timeout_seconds)
- `src/spec/resources/generated/elixir/lib/petstore_client/transport_options.ex:64` — timeout: non_neg_integer() | nil (typespec only, not enforced)

## F122 [medium] Per-operation server codegen emits duplicate types when two servers of one operation share a variable or a description
- Status: **fixed** (done via decision D42 in all SDKs (batches 5-6, branch parity/spec-expansion)) | Lens: L08-config | Category: codegen | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False
- SDKs: java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir

AbstractBetterCodegen.enrichOperationServers builds serverVariables per variant and never de-duplicates. Every api template emits the variable's enum inside the `{{#variants}}` loop. An operation with two servers that both declare an enum variable `region` is a normal pattern, for example `https://{region}.a.com` and `https://{region}.b.com`. It produces two declarations of the same enum type: compile errors in java (nested enum), kotlin, csharp (CS0101), go, dart, rust and swift; a TS duplicate identifier in node; silent last-wins redefinition in python and php (separate file overwritten), which is wrong if the enum sets differ; and a redefining-module warning in elixir and ruby, which elixir's --warnings-as-errors turns fatal. Variant names come from PascalCase(description) or `Server<index>`, so two servers with the same description, or one starting with a digit, also collide or produce invalid identifiers. The petstore only has getMultiServerPetInfo, where just one of the two servers has a variable, so this is untested.

- `src/main/resources/templates/java/api/api.mustache:52` — {{#variants}} {{#serverVariables}} {{#hasEnumValues}}         enum {{pascalName}} {
- `src/spec/resources/specs/petstore/openapi.yaml:911` — servers: - url: https://primary.example.com/v1 ... - url: https://{region}.example.com/v1

## F123 [medium] Test gaps: no test covers CA sole-anchor, garbage-CA rejection outside 3 SDKs, proxy failure classes, timeout <= 0, or a shared per-operation server variable
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L08-config | Category: test-gap | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir

These gaps let several findings above go unnoticed. (1) An unparseable CA file is tested only in java (garbagePemCaCertPathThrowsIllegalArgumentException), kotlin (ClientTest) and dart. The other 9 test only a missing file, so rust's lazy from_pem passes. Add a garbage-PEM row to every DefaultApiClient unit test. (2) Nothing checks that caCertPath is the sole trust anchor, so the dart/rust/ruby add-to-system-roots split goes unseen. Petstore/fixture expansion: point a client with caCertPath=fixtures/certs/ca.pem at a TLS endpoint signed by a different CA (a second chasm cert, or the publicly trusted proxy path) and expect NetworkError. (3) Proxy validation tests use one garbage string, except go (ftp, 'http://', socks5) and node (ftp). Missing-host, non-http scheme, upper-case scheme and empty-string cases are untested in 10 SDKs, and no SDK asserts the message. Add it.each/table rows to each TransportOptionsTest. (4) Negative/zero timeout is tested only in rust (test_transport_options_negative_timeout_is_rejected). (5) Server-variable message: no full-message assertion anywhere. (6) Petstore spec expansion: add an operation with two servers that share an enum variable (for example `https://{region}.a.example.com` and `https://{region}.b.example.com`), one with an undescribed server (a second `Server0` across operations, for csharp), and a URL template that repeats a variable. That catches the duplicate-type codegen defect, the csharp namespace collisions and node's first-occurrence replace. (7) swift: all HTTPS/CA/proxy integration tests sit under `#if !os(Linux)` and CI runs Linux, so the PEM-vs-DER, Linux-silent-TLS and HTTPSProxy-key bugs have zero coverage. A Linux-runnable unit test should at least assert that verifySsl(false) and caCertPath throw like proxyUnsupported.

- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L08-config | Category: api-shape | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True

dart cannot detect OpenTelemetry at runtime, so tracing works only if the application sets `TraceContextUtil.propagator = ...`, as the class doc says. ## F126 [medium] java, kotlin and swift trust only the first certificate in a caCertPath bundle
- Status: **fixed** (done in java, kotlin; still open for swift) | Lens: L08-config | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, swift

java and kotlin load the CA with CertificateFactory.generateCertificate(fis), which reads one certificate, and store a single 'ca' entry. swift calls SecCertificateCreateWithData once and anchors one certificate. The other 9 trust every certificate in the file: csharp ImportFromPemFile collection, go AppendCertsFromPEM, python load_verify_locations, ruby/php/elixir ca_file/cafile/cacertfile, node `ca` buffer, dart setTrustedCertificates, and rust (reqwest add_to_rustls iterates all PEM certs). A bundle with a root and an intermediate, or two roots during a CA rotation, works in 9 SDKs and fails TLS in java/kotlin/swift whenever the server chains to any cert but the first. The fix is generateCertificates() with every entry added to the trust store.

## F127 [medium] swift (Apple): an http:// proxy only covers http destinations, so HTTPS API calls bypass it
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L08-config | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False
- SDKs: swift

swift builds connectionProxyDictionary from the proxy URL's own scheme. For https://proxy it sets only HTTPSEnable/HTTPSProxy/HTTPSPort; for http://proxy it sets only HTTPEnable/HTTPProxy/HTTPPort. In CFNetwork, the HTTP* keys select the proxy for http:// requests and the HTTPS* keys select it for https:// requests. So with the usual http://proxy:3128, every https:// request goes direct, bypassing the proxy. With an https:// proxy URL, http:// requests go direct instead. Every other SDK sends all traffic through the configured proxy (java ProxySelector.of, go http.ProxyURL, node ProxyAgent, python ProxyManager, etc.). Only on Apple platforms; Linux throws proxyUnsupported, so CI never runs this path. Not runtime-verified here; based on CFNetwork key semantics.
- `src/spec/resources/generated/swift/Sources/PetstoreClient/DefaultApiClient.swift:828` — if scheme == "https" {           proxyDict["HTTPSEnable"] = true ... } else {           proxyDict["HTTPEnable"] = true
- `src/main/resources/templates/swift/default_api_client.mustache:804`

## F128 [medium] swift on Linux silently ignores verifySsl=false and caCertPath, while a proxy on Linux throws
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L08-config | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: swift

The whole URLSession server-trust challenge handler is inside `#if canImport(Security)`. On Linux (FoundationNetworking) there is no handler, so verifySsl(false) does not disable verification and caCertPath is not applied. Only the file's readability is checked, and the system trust store is used. Both settings are dropped without any error. For the comparable platform limit, swift throws ConfigurationError.proxyUnsupported when a proxy is configured on Linux. So swift is internally inconsistent, and on Linux it accepts settings that do nothing; the other 11 honour both. The platform limit is forced, but staying silent is not: it should throw like proxyUnsupported. Linux is the platform CI uses, and all swift HTTPS tests are excluded there.

Reviewer suspected this is forced: swift-corelibs-foundation does not surface server-trust challenges; forced to be unsupported, but not forced to be silent
- `src/spec/resources/generated/swift/Sources/PetstoreClient/DefaultApiClient.swift:968` — #if canImport(Security)     func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, didReceive challenge: ...
- `src/spec/resources/generated/swift/Sources/PetstoreClient/DefaultApiClient.swift:821` — #if os(Linux)       if opts.proxy != nil {         throw ConfigurationError.proxyUnsupported
- `src/spec/resources/generated/swift/Tests/PetstoreClientTests/DefaultApiClientTests.swift:15` — #if !os(Linux)

`foodType` is `required` in DryFood/WetFood. The generator gives it a synthetic default from the discriminator mapping (applyDiscriminatorDefault, AbstractBetterCodegen.java ~5640). Decoding a DryFood with no `foodType` key is then accepted and filled with 'dry' by java (field initializer, not a creator param), kotlin (`= "dry"`), csharp (not `required`), php (assertRequiredPresent skips defaulted ctor params), python (`default="dry"`), ruby (`Types::Required.default('dry')`), node (constructor fills it) and elixir (required_fields excludes it). Decide one rule (most likely: accept, because the default satisfies the requirement) and add a 'DryFood without foodType' decode test in all 12.

Fix: java should disable ACCEPT_FLOAT_AS_INT and set a CoercionConfig that fails Integer/Float to Textual; node should add `Number.isInteger` (or isSafeInteger) checks.

## F132 [medium] `format: uri` is a validated type in 6 SDKs and a plain string in 6; python's validator accepts only absolute http(s) URLs

Type mapping for URI: java java.net.URI, kotlin io.ktor.http.Url, csharp System.Uri, php \Uri\Rfc3986\Uri, python UrlStr, node branded URI (only a typeof check), and String in dart/go/rust/swift/ruby/elixir. AGENTS does not record this as forced, and swift (Foundation URL is Codable), dart (core Uri), ruby (URI) and elixir (URI) all have a stdlib URI type. The visible behavioural effect is in python: UrlStr validates through `TypeAdapter(HttpUrl)` (_types.py:25,62), which rejects valid RFC 3986 URIs. In pydantic 2.12, `urn:isbn:0451450523`, `mailto:a@b.com`, `ftp://x.org/f` and `/relative` are all rejected, so a Pet whose homepageUrl uses any non-http scheme fails to deserialize only in python. java URI.create rejects strings with spaces, while the string-typed SDKs accept anything. kotlin's `Url(String)` (KtorUrlSerializer, ObjectSerializer.kt:803) goes through URLBuilder.takeFrom, which normalizes relative or default-port inputs, so a re-encoded value may not be byte-identical. That last point is plausible but unverified here.

## F133 [medium] `type: number` (weightKg): python and node are lossy on decode (python on encode too) and accept quoted strings, contradicting AGENTS' 'FIVE preserve full textual precision'
- Status: **open** (documents corrected; the code or template part is still open) | Lens: L09-models-scalars | Category: doc-truth | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: python, node

AGENTS.md:246 lists python (`Decimal`) and node (branded `Decimal` + `JSON.rawJSON`) among the FIVE SDKs that preserve full precision. That is not true of the code. python decodes with a plain `json.loads` without `parse_float=Decimal` (object_serializer.py:220), so the value is a binary float before pydantic builds the Decimal. In pydantic 2.12, `{"weightKg": 0.1234567890123456789}` gives `Decimal('0.12345678901234568')` and 12345678901234567890.5 gives `Decimal('12345678901234567000')`. Encoding goes through `float(value)` (_types.py:87-90). node decodes with a bare `JSON.parse` (object-serializer.ts:274), so the number is already rounded before the Pet constructor applies `String(this.weightKg)` (pet.ts:161-162). Both also accept a JSON STRING for a `type: number` field. python's Decimal is lax, so `"12.345"` is accepted. node accepts ANY string (`"abc"`), because the only check is `typeof !== "string"` (pet.ts:163), and it then re-emits it quoted. java/kotlin/csharp reject a quoted number (jackson 2.19.4 with ALLOW_COERCION_OF_SCALARS=false gives MismatchedInputException; kotlin's BigDecimal(element.toString()) fails on the quotes). The python README even claims the field 'deserializes to decimal.Decimal' as the precision-safe path. Either fix decoding (python `parse_float=decimal.Decimal`; node a JSON.parse reviver using `context.source`) or move both to the lossy list in AGENTS.

- `src/spec/resources/generated/python/petstore_client/_types.py:89` — PlainSerializer(lambda value: float(value), return_type=float, when_used="json"),

## F135 [medium] node's global Decimal-field registry turns string values in free-form objects into JSON numbers when their key matches any model's decimal field name
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L09-models-scalars | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True

ObjectSerializer.serialize's replacer (object-serializer.ts:360-372) checks the holder's constructor for `__decimalFields`. The other 11 SDKs never change the JSON type of a free-form value. In a real spec with a common decimal name (`amount`, `price`), every free-form payload using that key is corrupted.

## F140 [medium] additionalProperties are lost on nested models (and in kotlin, on list elements): only a top-level model captures and re-emits extras
- Status: **deferred** | Lens: L10-models-composed | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True

kotlin calls populateAdditionalProperties(decoded, raw) and mergeAdditionalProperties(encoded, unwrapped) only on the root object. A Metadata nested inside another model, or inside a List<Metadata> response, decodes with ignoreUnknownKeys and drops its extras; on encode, a nested model's @Transient bucket is never merged back. node re-attaches extras via `__additionalPropertiesDeclaredKeys` only after the root plainToInstance; nested @Type models built by class-transformer use excludeExtraneousValues and lose them. Arrays re-enter deserialize, so they are fine. php calls captureAdditionalProperties only on the class handed to deserializeInternal. Nested objects are denormalized by Symfony directly, so extras are dropped, and the sanitizeForSerialization flatten (lines 193-205) only lifts the ROOT object's `additionalProperties`. java (@JsonAnySetter/@JsonAnyGetter), csharp ([JsonExtensionData]), python (model_validator/serializer), ruby/elixir (recursive deserialize_model/sanitize), go/rust/swift/dart (per-type (Un)MarshalJSON/flatten/Codable/fromJson) handle nesting. The petstore never nests an additionalProperties model (Metadata is not referenced by any schema or operation), so nothing catches this. Expand the petstore: add `metadata: $ref Metadata` to Photo or PetPassport and an op returning `array of Metadata`. Then round-trip a nested extra key in all 12.

## F142 [medium] go matches JSON object keys case-insensitively: it accepts mis-cased keys the other 11 ignore, and double-captures them as additionalProperties
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L10-models-composed | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True

Every go model's UnmarshalJSON decodes into `type Alias X` with encoding/json, which matches struct tags case-insensitively. `{"name":"d","photoUrls":[],"STATUS":"sold"}` therefore sets Pet.Status. The required-field and additionalProperties checks look up `raw["…"]` case-sensitively, so the two disagree. For Metadata, `{"CreatedAt":"2024-01-01T00:00:00.000+00:00"}` sets CreatedAt AND stores `CreatedAt` in AdditionalProperties. Re-marshalling then emits both `createdAt` and `CreatedAt`. With duplicate differently-cased keys, go keeps the last one. A discriminator spelled `FOODTYPE` also routes in go. The other 11 (Jackson default, kotlinx, System.Text.Json with PropertyNameCaseInsensitive unset, pydantic, Symfony SerializedName, ruby/elixir/dart/node exact maps, serde, Codable) are case-sensitive. A mis-cased key is unknown to them: ignored, or captured only as an additional property. Not forced: the models already unmarshal `raw map[string]json.RawMessage` and could drop non-exact keys (or use encoding/json/v2's case-sensitive matching). Not documented in AGENTS. Unit-testable: decode a mis-cased key into Pet and Metadata.

Reviewer suspected this is forced: encoding/json v1 is case-insensitive by design. It is avoidable because each model already has the exact raw key map.

## F144 [medium] A bare JSON `null` 200 body on a body-returning operation behaves four different ways: silent null (csharp), raw TypeError (dart), silent nil/zero success (go collections/maps), SerializationError (rust/go structs), versus the empty-body ApiException elsewhere
- Status: **fixed** (done in csharp, dart; still open for go, rust) | Lens: L11-api-shape | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: csharp, dart, go, rust

kotlin's ObjectSerializer documents the intended rule: a top-level `null` is an absent body. That makes data null, and the convenience method throws the canonical `Expected a response body for <op> but received none` ApiException. java/python/ruby/php/node/swift/elixir reach the same result because their parsers map `null` to null/nil/None. csharp's convenience method gates on `string.IsNullOrEmpty(result.RawBody)`. RawBody is "null" (non-empty), so it returns `result.Data!`, a null Pet from a non-nullable `Task<Pet>`, with no error. dart's generated deserialize closure is `(body) => deserialize(body, Pet.fromJson) as Pet`. ObjectSerializer.deserialize returns null for `null`, and `null as Pet` throws a dart TypeError, a non-SDK type, from inside invokeApiForResult, before the convenience check that exists to avoid exactly that TypeError. go's WithHTTPInfo sets `dataPtr = &data` whenever Body != "". json.Unmarshal(`null`) is a no-op for slices/maps/scalars, so FindPetsByStatus/GetInventory return a non-nil pointer to a nil slice/map as success. Pet fails in its custom UnmarshalJSON with a 'required field missing' error instead. rust's serde rejects null for Pet/Vec, giving a SerializationError rather than the empty-body ApiError. The test suites only cover an empty `""` body, never `null`. Fix: treat a bare `null` as an absent body in csharp (also check Data is null), dart (make the closure null-tolerant), go (leave dataPtr nil when the payload is `null`) and rust (map Value::Null to None). Add a `200 application/json "null"` case next to each language's testEmptyBodyOnBodyReturningOperationThrows.

## F145 [medium] All 12: a server-variable enum type is emitted once per VARIANT, so two variants of the same operation that share a variable name (or a description) generate duplicate types
- Status: **fixed** (done via decision D42 in all SDKs (batches 5-6, branch parity/spec-expansion)) | Lens: L11-api-shape | Category: codegen | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False
- SDKs: java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir

AbstractBetterCodegen.enrichOperationServers builds `serverVariables` per variant, and every template emits the enum inside `{{#variants}}{{#serverVariables}}{{#hasEnumValues}}` as `{{serverTypeName}}{{pascalName}}` (or a nested `{{pascalName}}`), which does not include the variant. For an operation with servers `https://{region}.a.example` and `https://{region}.b.example` (a common multi-region pattern), each language emits the region enum twice. The result is a compile error in java (duplicate nested enum), kotlin, csharp, go, rust, swift and dart, and a duplicate `export enum` in node. elixir gets a module redefinition, fatal under --warnings-as-errors. php regenerates the same file and the last write silently wins. ruby/python silently redefine the module/class. variantName is derived only from the description (else `Server<i>`), so two variants with the same description also collide in all 12. The petstore never has two variants sharing a variable, so nothing catches this. Fix: dedupe variable enums per operation in the codegen (merge enum values or name per variant) and disambiguate duplicate variantNames. Spec expansion: add a second `{region}` variant to getMultiServerPetInfo.

## F147 [medium] go: every operation's primary doc comment is detached from its func (blank line), so godoc/gopls/staticcheck never see it — including the `// Deprecated:` marker on FindPetsByStatus/GetPetById, which is also not its own paragraph
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L11-api-shape | Category: docs | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: go

The go api template ends the data-method doc block with `{{#allParams}}{{#vendorExtensions.pluralExamples}}` on one line (two tags, so jmustache does not treat it as standalone). That emits a blank line between the `//` comment block and `func`. Go only treats a comment as a doc comment when it sits directly above the declaration with no blank line, so every data method (AddPet, GetPetByName, FindPetsByStatus, GetPetById, all StoreApi data methods) has NO doc comment. Two consequences: (1) `// Deprecated: This operation is deprecated.` on the primary FindPetsByStatus/GetPetById methods is not attached, so staticcheck SA1019 and gopls never flag callers; only the *WithHTTPInfo variants (which emit a correct `//` + `// Deprecated:` paragraph) are flagged. (2) Even attached, the marker sits mid-paragraph (line 678 directly after the summary, with no `//` separator line). Go's convention and staticcheck's parser only recognise a paragraph that STARTS with `Deprecated: `. The same mid-paragraph form appears on deprecated Options fields (`/* Status ... */` immediately followed by `// Deprecated:`), so FindPetsByStatusOptions.Status is not recognised as deprecated either. This contradicts the AGENTS T2-5 claim that go marks every public variant with a `// Deprecated:` doc paragraph. Fix: make the examples line standalone (or put the loop inside a single section), emit `//` before `// Deprecated:` as the WithHTTPInfo branch already does, and do the same in options.mustache. ## F148 [medium] ruby and elixir: per-operation server variables are plain strings with no enum validation, so any string is placed into the request host (the global ServerConfiguration rejects it)
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L11-api-shape | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: ruby, elixir

In 10 languages a per-op server variant with enum variables can only be built from the enum type. java/kotlin/swift/rust/dart/php/csharp enforce this in the type system or at runtime; python's `.value` access fails on a raw str. ruby's `GetStagingPetInfoServerStagingServer.new(environment:, version:)` and elixir's `%GetStagingPetInfoServer.StagingServer{environment:, version:}` accept any string and gsub it straight into `https://{environment}.example.com/api/{version}`. The 'enum' is only a module of constants (ruby) or zero-arity functions (elixir). For example `environment: 'attacker.net/x#'` redirects the request, client credentials included, to another host without error. The same SDKs' global ServerConfiguration DOES raise ArgumentError for a value outside the enum, and AGENTS lists "a server variable outside its enum" as a caller mistake that must raise the built-in error. Fix: validate against the declared enum in the ruby initializer and in the elixir url/1 (raise ArgumentError with the global-config wording). Add a ruby/elixir unit test that an out-of-enum value raises.

## F150 [medium] A response with no Content-Type on a byte/binary operation (getPetAvatar, downloadPetDocument, getPetAvatarThumbnail) decodes differently everywhere
- Status: **open** | Lens: L12-api-bodies | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir

Every transport treats an absent Content-Type as text and returns the UTF-8-decoded string. The API layers then disagree. For a format:binary operation such as getPetAvatar: java base64-decodes that text and throws a raw IllegalArgumentException (see the separate java finding). kotlin, csharp and ruby return the UTF-8 bytes. dart tries base64 first and falls back to UTF-8. python, node, go, swift and elixir assume JSON and raise SerializationError. rust parses it as JSON and returns an EMPTY Vec on failure. php json_decode()s it to null, then settype(null,'string') gives "", which is returned as the bytes with no error. For a format:byte operation such as getPetAvatarThumbnail, whose body is a JSON string literal: python, ruby, node, php, go, rust, swift and elixir default to JSON and decode correctly. kotlin, csharp and dart return the UTF-8 bytes of the QUOTED literal, which are wrong bytes. java throws IllegalArgumentException. The dart result contradicts AGENTS 'dart defaults an absent/empty response Content-Type to JSON … matching swift/node' for byte returns. Root cause: binary and byte returns collapse to one native type, and the base layer is not told which format the operation declared. Fix: have the generator pass isBinary/isByteArray to the base layer and apply one rule. Add unit tests for both operations with no Content-Type.

## F151 [medium] Malformed base64 in a top-level format:byte response (getPetAvatarThumbnail): 3 raw platform exceptions, 2 silent decodes, contradicting AGENTS T1-10
- Status: **open** | Lens: L12-api-bodies | Category: error-contract | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, csharp, dart, node, rust

getPetAvatarThumbnail returns a JSON string literal holding base64. If that string is not valid base64, the error contract says every decode failure is a SerializationError. python, ruby, php, go, swift and elixir raise it. java and kotlin call java.util.Base64.getDecoder().decode(inner) outside any wrapper, so a raw IllegalArgumentException leaks. csharp's Convert.FromBase64String leaks a raw FormatException, and dart's base64Decode(inner) does the same. node uses `Buffer.from(json as string, 'base64')`, which silently drops non-alphabet characters: I confirmed that "!!not*base64??" decodes to 6 garbage bytes. rust does `.decode(...).unwrap_or_default()` and returns an EMPTY Vec. AGENTS.md (Resolved) says 'python and node reject malformed base64 on decode (node decodeBase64 validates …) matching ruby/php/elixir/go/rust'. The node top-level byte path never calls decodeBase64, and rust's top-level path is lenient, so the code contradicts that document. R7-T3 covers only model fields, not this operation-return path. Fix: route these decodes through each SDK's strict decoder or SerializationError wrapper, and add a malformed-thumbnail unit test in all 12.

(b) An operation whose only response is `default` with a schema, plus a 4xx response with a declared error schema; no petstore operation declares an error-response schema or a default response, so the codegen path for operation-declared error bodies is uncovered. (c) Unit tests (no spec change needed) driving getPetPhoto with the application/json Photo variant, and getPetAvatar/getPetAvatarThumbnail with no Content-Type and with malformed base64. (g) date-time, number and boolean fields on setPetPreferences, which would catch ruby's to_s. (h) An exact-order assertion on form and multipart bodies in every language. ## F153 [medium] java BaseApi treats an empty Content-Type as base64-binary while its own transport treats it as text
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L12-api-bodies | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java

Java's DefaultApiClient.isTextContentType("") returns true, with the comment 'A response with no Content-Type defaults to text handling', so the body is a UTF-8 String. BaseApi.isTextResponseContentType("") returns false, and its comment says 'Mirror the transport: an absent/empty Content-Type is treated as binary (base64-encoded by the transport)'. That is false. So getPetAvatar, downloadPetDocument and getPetPhoto with no Content-Type call Base64.getDecoder().decode() on decoded text. The result is a raw IllegalArgumentException leaking past the error contract, or garbage bytes when the text happens to be base64-shaped. kotlin, csharp, ruby, python and go mirror their transports correctly: all return true for empty. Fix: return true for empty in java's base_api.mustache, and add a unit test with a binary operation and no Content-Type.

## F154 [medium] kotlin void operations throw when the success response carries a non-object body
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L12-api-bodies | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: kotlin

Kotlin routes void operations (deletePet, setPetAvatar, setPetAvatarThumbnail) through invokeApiForResult<Unit>, and that function decodes any non-empty body. A text/plain or octet-stream body (for example `200 OK` with body "Deleted") hits the non-JSON branch `response.body as T`. Because T is reified Unit, that is a checked cast, so a raw java.lang.ClassCastException escapes the SDK. A JSON body that is not an object (`true`, `[]`, `"ok"`) makes deserialize<Unit> throw SerializationException. The other 11 never decode a void operation's body: java, csharp, python, ruby, node, dart, go and elixir pass a null or empty returnType, rust and swift use invoke…ForEmptyResult, and php only populates data, per T3-15. Fix: skip decoding when T is Unit, as java does by passing returnType null. Add a void-op-with-text-body unit test to every language.

## F155 [medium] rust and go return an empty string for a String-returning operation that gets a text/plain body
- Status: **partial** (done in rust; still open for go) | Lens: L12-api-bodies | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: rust, go

Every transport keeps text/* bodies as decoded text: rust's is_text_content_type returns true for text/*. Yet rust's invoke_api_for_result non-JSON, non-binary branch assumes the body was base64-encoded and calls STANDARD.decode(body).unwrap_or_default(). Any text containing a space or other non-base64 character decodes to nothing, so the caller gets Some(""). Text that happens to be valid base64 decodes to garbage. go's per-operation response template only has branches for JSON and []byte, so a string (or model) return with a text/* Content-Type keeps its zero value and returns "" or a zero struct with a nil error. java, kotlin, csharp, python, ruby, node, php, dart, swift and elixir return the text verbatim, and java/kotlin/csharp/python have a test for it (returnsRawStringForNonJson). This is latent in the petstore goldens because testTextPlain is x-internal and never generated, so no public operation returns text/plain and the rust/go code paths are never exercised. Fix: rust should return the body as-is for text media types; go should add a string branch. Expose a public text/plain operation in petstore so all 12 compile and test this path.

## F160 [medium] rust has no brotli decode test, and no SDK asserts the Accept-Encoding it advertises by default
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L13a-tests-transport | Category: test-gap | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: rust, java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, go, swift, elixir

Eleven SDKs have a 'decompresses brotli response' integration test; rust has gzip and zstd only, although T3-6 added a 'br' arm (brotli::Decompressor) and 'br' to rust's Accept-Encoding and called it 'CI-validated' - nothing exercises it. ## F161 [medium] swift depth-cap test uses 50-deep 'within' (peers 500-600) and its comment contradicts the source and AGENTS; Foundation's ~512 nesting limit makes swift's effective cap <1000
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L13a-tests-transport | Category: test-gap | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: swift

Ten SDKs assert a 600-deep payload decodes and 1500-deep is rejected (rust 500/1500). swift asserts only nestedObjects(50) decodes. Its comment says swift 'relies on the platform decoder's guard rather than a 1000-deep pre-flight cap', which contradicts the swift source (ObjectSerializer.maxJsonDepth = 1000 with a jsonMaxDepth pre-flight) and AGENTS R6-6 ('all 12 use the 1000 depth cap'). ## F166 [medium] Space-encoding assertions accept either `+` or `%20` in 7 SDKs, so the authorize-URL `%20` and token-body `+` contracts are not locked
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L13b-tests-api-auth-models | Category: test-gap | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, csharp, python, go, rust, elixir, dart, swift

The resolved contract is `%20` in the authorize URL (php T1-1) and `+` in the x-www-form-urlencoded token body. For the authorize URL, php, ruby, node, dart and swift assert `scope=read%20write` exactly. java, kotlin and elixir accept `+` or `%20`, and csharp also accepts a raw space. python parses the URL with parse_qs, so `+` and `%20` look the same. go and rust check only `scope=read`. For the token body (`sendsScopes`), csharp, php, ruby and rust assert `scope=read+write`. java, kotlin, python and elixir accept either encoding (python also a raw space). dart, go and swift check only `scope=read` plus `write`. node compares the decoded value, which cannot tell the encodings apart. A regression to a default RFC 1738 encoder in the authorize URL, the T1-1 bug class, would pass in 7 SDKs. Fix: assert the exact encoded substring in every SDK, matching the php/ruby/node/dart/swift authorize tests and the csharp/php/ruby/rust body tests.

## F171 [medium] Component-level enum defaults on a $ref property: ignored by java/kotlin/php/python, emitted as an untyped string literal by 8 others
- Status: **open** | Lens: L14-codegen-java | Category: codegen | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, php, python, csharp, dart, node, rust, swift, go, ruby, elixir

java, kotlin, php and python resolve the default through ModelUtils.unaliasSchema. Upstream keeps a $ref to an enum schema unchanged there (ModelUtils.java:1409 `isEnumSchema(ref) ... return schema`), so getDefault() returns null and the enum component's default is dropped. csharp, dart, elixir, go, node, ruby, rust and swift resolve it through ModelUtils.getReferencedSchema and do pick up the default. Because such a property has isEnumRef rather than isEnum, fixEnumDefaultValue and updateCodegenPropertyEnum never turn it into an enum member. The result is a plain string literal assigned to an enum-typed field: node `'medium'` to an enum (TS2322), dart `'medium'` (type error), swift `"medium"` (type error), rust `String::from("medium")` (E0308), and csharp the bare token `medium` under the `global::...Models.` prefix (csharp/models/model.mustache:491). Only go (untyped string constant), ruby and elixir (`:"medium"`) come out correct. Not exercised by petstore, which has no $ref'd enum with a default.
