- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L06-simple-auth | Category: api-shape | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False
- SDKs: ruby

`SessionCookieAuthenticator.new(host:, api_key:)`, `AdminBasicAuthenticator.new(host:, username:, password:)` and `ServiceTokenAuthenticator.new(host:, token:)` are keyword-only. The bases they subclass are positional (`ApiKeyAuthenticator.new(host, key_param_name, api_key, location)`, `BearerAuthenticator.new(host, token)`). So `ServiceTokenAuthenticator.new('h','t')` raises ArgumentError, while the matching base call works. In java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, node, go, rust, swift and elixir the wrappers are positional like their bases. dart is named everywhere, which is consistent within dart. The RBS sig matches the code, so steep does not catch the mismatch, and no test constructs a ruby wrapper. Fix: pick one convention for ruby and use it for both base and wrapper.

## F284 [low] rust appends authenticator query params instead of overriding, so a same-named query parameter is sent twice
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L06-simple-auth | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: rust

The other 11 SDKs merge `getQueryParams()` into a map keyed by name (java put, python update, go map assign, dart addAll, elixir Map.merge, ...), so the authenticator's api_key replaces any same-named operation query parameter and the URL carries exactly one `api_key=`. rust keeps a Vec of tuples and `push`es the authenticator's entries, so the URL carries both `api_key=<user>&api_key=<secret>`, and which value wins depends on the server. This is latent: no petstore operation has a query parameter named after the apiKeyQuery scheme (`api_key`). To pin it, add a petstore or probe operation secured by apiKeyQuery that also declares an optional `in: query, name: api_key` parameter, and assert a single occurrence. Fix: remove any existing entry with the same key before pushing.

## F292 [low] Token-request body and authorize-URL parameter order differ (java hash order, go/elixir sorted, rust/swift random per process)

Same input, different bytes. kotlin/csharp/php/python/ruby/node/dart emit insertion order (grant_type, client_id, client_secret, scope). java builds params in HashMap and iterates hash order: grant_type, scope, client_secret, client_id (computed). go url.Values.Encode() and elixir URI.encode_query(map) sort keys (client_id, client_secret, grant_type, scope; authorize URL client_id, redirect_uri, response_type, scope, state). rust (HashMap with RandomState) and swift (Dictionary with per-process seeded hashing) change the order between runs, so their token bodies are non-deterministic. Semantically equivalent for a form decoder, but it violates the byte-identical rule and makes byte-level golden assertions impossible. Use insertion-ordered containers (LinkedHashMap, ordered slice, Vec, KeyValuePairs, keyword list).

node's per-operation server variants substitute with `url.replace("{" + name + "}", value)`, which replaces only the first occurrence. ## F312 [low] elixir's model-level `@deprecated` attaches to the next function (defstruct's __struct__), not to the module
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L09-models-scalars | Category: docs | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False
- SDKs: elixir

elixir/models/model.mustache:332-334 (and :490-492) emit `@deprecated "This schema is deprecated."` just before `@type t` and `defstruct`. In Elixir, @deprecated is a function attribute: it applies to the next `def`, and defstruct expands to `def __struct__/0,1`. The deprecation therefore lands on __struct__ (or the next generated function), which users never call directly; `%Tag{}` expands at compile time and gives no warning, and the module is not marked deprecated in docs. The idiomatic module-level marker is `@moduledoc deprecated: "…"` (doc metadata), which is close to the R6-3 moduledoc approach. The other 11 SDKs mark the type itself. This is plausible from reasoning; elixir is not available locally to verify.
- `src/spec/resources/generated/elixir/lib/petstore_client/models/tag.ex:13` — @deprecated "This schema is deprecated."
- `src/main/resources/templates/elixir/models/model.mustache:333`

## F316 [low] ruby (Types::Any) and elixir models do no type or enum validation on construction, and go enums never validate on encode, so wrong-typed values reach the wire

Every optional ruby attribute is `Types::Any.optional` (e.g. pet.rb:81, order.rb:68-77). Required ones are `Types::Required`, which only checks non-nil. Only INLINE enums use `Types::String.enum`, and $ref enums (favorite_color, availability) are Any. So `Pet.new(name: 123, photo_urls: [1])` or `Order.new(quantity: 'x')` builds and serializes `"name":123` with no error. OPENAPI_TYPES checking runs only on deserialize. elixir structs are untyped, and sanitize_for_serialization emits whatever is stored: an unknown inline-enum atom goes out as its name, and an unknown standalone-enum atom hits a FunctionClauseError in value/1. go enum types have UnmarshalJSON validation but no MarshalJSON, so `OrderStatusEnum("bogus")` is sent. python validates on construction and assignment (validate_assignment), node in the constructor, php through typed properties, and the static languages through their types.

## F317 [low] ruby request bodies send a DateTime in non-canonical form because `when Date` matches DateTime first
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L09-models-scalars | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: ruby

In sanitize_for_serialization, `when Date` (object_serializer.rb:275) comes before `when Time, DateTime` (:282). DateTime is a subclass of Date, so a DateTime value takes the Date branch and is sent as `object.to_s`, i.e. `2024-01-01T12:30:45+00:00` with no `.000`, instead of DEFAULT_DATETIME_FORMAT `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%3N%:z`. Verified with ruby: `case DateTime.new(...) when Date` matches. The DateTime half of the second arm is dead code. Model attributes are `Types::Any`, so a DateTime assigned to a date-time field such as Order.ship_date reaches this path. The parameter path (stringify, :187) has no Date arm and is correct.

## F339 [low] Form-urlencoded and multipart field order on the wire differs (hash order, sorted, or random per process)
- Status: **open** | Lens: L12-api-bodies | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, go, swift, elixir, rust

setPetPreferences fields are nickname, tags, note, renewalDate in spec order. kotlin, csharp, python, ruby, node, php, dart and rust emit them in spec/insertion order. java builds the body in a HashMap, so the order is note, nickname, renewalDate, tags (verified on the JDK). go's url.Values.Encode and elixir's small-map Enum both sort keys: nickname, note, renewalDate, tags. swift iterates a [String: Any], which is randomly seeded per process. For multipart (uploadPetDocument: file, documentType, notes): java sends file, notes, documentType; elixir sorts; go (`range formFields` over a map), rust (HashMap<String, MultipartValue>) and swift ([String: Any]) are non-deterministic per call or per process. The governing rule asks for the same bytes on the wire. Ordered multipart matters to streaming servers that expect metadata before the file. kotlin, csharp and rust tests assert the exact order; java, swift, php, node and dart only assert contains(). Fix: use LinkedHashMap, ordered pairs or an ordered dict, and assert the exact body in every language.

## F343 [low] csharp sends `application/json; charset=utf-8` (and form `; charset=utf-8`) where the other 11 send the bare declared type
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L12-api-bodies | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False
- SDKs: csharp

csharp's DefaultApiClient wraps string bodies, meaning every JSON and form-urlencoded request, in `new StringContent(text, Encoding.UTF8, contentType)`. On .NET 8 that sets Content-Type to `<type>; charset=utf-8`. The override that applies the declared type explicitly excludes strings (`body is not string`). The multipart JSON part (`new(json, Encoding.UTF8, "application/json")`) and the redirect-replay path behave the same way. Every other SDK puts the declared type on the wire verbatim. The file already strips StringContent's default Content-Type from multipart text parts 'to keep the multipart wire bytes identical across languages', so this is not forced. Tests capture headers at the IApiClient seam, before HttpClient, so they never see the charset. Fix: set Headers.ContentType = new MediaTypeHeaderValue(contentType) after construction.

## F344 [low] ruby form-urlencoded body stringifies values with to_s instead of ObjectSerializer
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L12-api-bodies | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: ruby

Ruby's serialize_body sends form bodies through `URI.encode_www_form(body.compact)`, which calls to_s on each value, and the operation layer passes raw values (for example `request_body['renewalDate'] = options.renewal_date`). The other 11 stringify form values through their canonical helper: java toFormValue, kotlin/csharp/python/node/dart/go/swift/elixir stringify, php's formatDateOnly pre-format, and rust serde values. Ruby's own query path uses ObjectSerializer.to_query_value, so ruby is inconsistent with itself as well. It is latent in petstore because Date#to_s happens to be YYYY-MM-DD. A date-time form field would go out as `2024-01-01 12:00:00 UTC` instead of the canonical `.SSS+00:00`, and a BigDecimal as `0.15e1`. A nil element inside an array produces a bare `tags` key, where the others skip it. Expand setPetPreferences with date-time, number and boolean fields to cover this.

## F363 [low] Whitespace-only / symbol-only enum values: php alone avoids an empty identifier
- Status: **fixed** (done via decision D43 in all SDKs (batches 5-6, branch parity/spec-expansion)) | Lens: L14-codegen-java | Category: codegen | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: php, java, kotlin, csharp, go, rust, swift, dart, python, ruby, node, elixir

In AbstractBetterCodegen.toEnumVarName, sanitizeName(" ") gives "_", and stripping the leading and trailing underscore then leaves "". An enum value made only of spaces, or one that sanitizes to nothing (for example `@@`, or non-ASCII text without allowUnicodeIdentifiers), therefore gets an empty constant name and the generated SDK fails to compile in 11 languages. Only BetterPHPCodegen.toEnumVarName handles a subset of this, mapping whitespace-only values to `SPACE_<n>`. There is no shared fallback such as `VALUE_<index>`, and no language disambiguates enum constants that collide after casing (`a-b` vs `a_b`).

Reviewer suspected this is forced: None. The php fix belongs in the shared base.

## F383 [low] SwiftFormattingSpec runs swift-format lint without --strict, so it exits 0 on any formatting finding
- Status: **open** | Lens: L17-gates | Category: gate | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False
- SDKs: swift

swift-format lint reports findings as warnings and exits non-zero only when `--strict` is passed. SwiftFormattingSpec.generatedCodeShouldBeProperlyFormatted runs `swift-format lint --recursive Sources Tests` without it, so the test cannot fail on a formatting violation. Every other language's formatting spec exits non-zero on drift (`--check`, `--set-exit-if-changed`, `--check-formatted`, `test -z $(gofmt -l)`). Formatting is still covered, because SwiftLintingSpec runs `swift-format lint --strict`. The formatting spec itself is just a check that always passes, and a swift formatting regression is reported as a linting failure, not a formatting one.

## F385 [low] Multipart JSON part headers differ: csharp and dart add `; charset=utf-8` and change header order; kotlin adds a per-part Content-Length

For addPetPhotos, the `metadata` part (encoding contentType application/json) is sent by java, python, ruby, php, node, go, rust, swift, elixir and kotlin as `Content-Disposition: form-data; name="metadata"` followed by `Content-Type: application/json`. csharp builds it with `new StringContent(json, Encoding.UTF8, "application/json")`, which sets `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8`. Because Content-Disposition is removed and re-added afterwards, the Content-Type header also comes first. csharp already avoids this default for scalar parts (a comment in DefaultApiClient explains it), but not for the JSON part. dart uses `http.MultipartFile.fromString(..., contentType: MediaType('application','json'))`, and package:http always adds a charset parameter there, so dart also sends `application/json; charset=utf-8`. package:http also writes content-type before content-disposition and gives non-ASCII text fields an extra `content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8` and `content-transfer-encoding: binary`. kotlin: Ktor's formData adds a `Content-Length` header to each binary part (checked with ktor-client-core 3.5.0: `[Content-Disposition=[form-data; name="files", filename="files"], Content-Type=[image/png], Content-Length=[2]]`). No other SDK sends a per-part Content-Length. AGENTS closes only the multipart filename and MIME type and kotlin's test depth, not these header bytes.

## F386 [low] Query, form and multipart parameter order is not the declared order in 7 languages: hash order, random or sorted
- Status: **open** | Lens: L18a-wire-request | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, go, swift, ruby, elixir, rust, python, dart

Kotlin, csharp, php, node, dart (query and form) and rust (query and form) send query parameters, form fields and multipart parts in declaration order. The other 7 do not, and four of them send different bytes on different calls. java uses `new HashMap<>()` for queryParams, formBody and multipart, so getPetTag sends `filter,sizes,colors,revision`, setPetPreferences sends `note,nickname,renewalDate,tags`, addPetPhotos sends `metadata` before `files`, and uploadPetDocument sends `file,notes,documentType` (Java HashMap order computed). go ranges over a `map[string]any`, so query and multipart order is randomized per call; its form body is sorted by url.Values.Encode. swift iterates `[String: Any?]` dictionaries, so query and form order is randomized per process (two runs gave different orders). ruby is re-sorted alphabetically by Faraday (previous finding). elixir iterates small maps in sorted key order (query, form and multipart). rust multipart uses `HashMap<String, MultipartValue>`, which is randomized. python sends every allowReserved parameter after all the others. dart's http.MultipartRequest writes every text field before every file or JSON part. Ordered containers exist in every one of these languages (LinkedHashMap, slices, Vec, KeyValuePairs, keyword lists), and rust already uses an ordered Vec for query and form, so no language feature forces the difference.

## F387 [low] allowReserved characters are re-escaped by the HTTP client in node and rust (') and swift ([ ])
- Status: **open** | Lens: L18a-wire-request | Category: wire | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False
- SDKs: node, rust, swift, php

The allowReserved encoders all restore the same reserved set `: / ? # [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) * + , ; =`, but some HTTP clients re-parse the URL and change those bytes before sending. node passes the URL to fetch, whose WHATWG parser escapes `'` as %27 in an http(s) query (checked: `new URL('http://h/p?k=a'b')` → `k=a%27b`). rust passes it through `reqwest::Url::parse`, which implements the same WHATWG rule. swift's `URL(string:)` escapes `[` and `]` in the query (checked on macOS: `revision=a[b]` → `revision=a%5Bb%5D`). php builds the request through a PSR-7 Uri, and nyholm/psr7 query filtering escapes characters outside unreserved, sub-delims and `:@/?`, so `[` and `]` are likely escaped there too (not executed here). java, kotlin, csharp, python, go, dart and elixir keep their own bytes; ruby re-escapes everything (separate finding). The petstore example `v1.0/beta:rc1` comes through intact everywhere except ruby. Values containing `'`, `[` or `]` do not.

For setPetPreferences, the same input produces different body bytes across SDKs. java builds `Map<String, Object> formBody = new HashMap<>()`, so field order follows hash order. swift builds `var formBody: [String: Any]` and Swift Dictionary iteration is seeded per process, so the body bytes differ from run to run. go's `url.Values.Encode()` sorts keys alphabetically (nickname, note, renewalDate, tags). elixir's small maps iterate in key order. python/ruby/node/dart/php keep insertion order (nickname, tags, note, renewalDate). ## F398 [low] ApiResult equality and header mutability differ across the 12
- Status: **open** | Lens: L21-api-surface | Category: api-shape | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: csharp, ruby, dart, rust, swift, node, go, python, kotlin

ApiResult is the public return type of every `*WithHttpInfo` call, and its equality and immutability differ by language.
- Value equality: java (record), kotlin (data class), python (frozen dataclass), elixir (struct), php (loose ==).
- Reference equality: csharp (plain primary-ctor class, not a record), ruby, dart.
- No equality at all: rust (no PartialEq derive), swift (no Equatable conformance), node (plain interface object), go (map field makes == invalid).
- Headers: java and csharp take a read-only defensive copy, ruby freezes, rust, swift, php and elixir are immutable. python keeps a mutable `Dict` inside a `frozen=True` dataclass, so `hash(result)` raises TypeError and `result.headers[...] = ...` mutates it; python's own Configuration uses MappingProxyType for the same purpose. dart stores the mutable `response.headers` map as-is. kotlin stores the caller's map without copying.
None of this is forced: csharp can use `record`, rust can `derive(PartialEq)` (bounded on T), swift can add a conditional `Equatable where T: Equatable`, dart can override ==, and python/dart can wrap the headers read-only.

## F399 [low] Model equality on format:number fields depends on scale in java, kotlin and node, but not in csharp, python or the 7 float SDKs
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L21-api-surface | Category: model | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, kotlin, node

All 12 give models value equality, but the same two values compare differently. java's generated equals uses `Objects.equals(this.weightKg, other.weightKg)` on a BigDecimal, and kotlin's data class uses BigDecimal.equals. Both depend on scale: `1.5` and `1.50` are unequal and hash differently, so Pets decoded from `{"weightKg":1.5}` and `{"weightKg":1.50}` (Jackson keeps the text's scale) are not equal. node's Decimal is a branded string compared by `===`, so a user-built `Decimal("1.50")` does not equal a decoded `1.5` (JSON.parse canonicalises it to "1.5"). csharp (`decimal` equality and hash), python (verified: `Decimal('1.5') == Decimal('1.50')` with equal hashes) and the seven native-float SDKs treat them as equal. Not forced: java and kotlin can compare with `compareTo == 0` and hash `stripTrailingZeros()`, and node can normalise the Decimal string.

## F400 [low] Per-scheme authenticator wrappers differ in type hierarchy and printed form: java delegates, rust has no Debug, go and node print the base name
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L21-api-surface | Category: api-shape | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: java, rust, go, node

In kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, dart and swift a per-scheme authenticator subclasses the generic one (`PetStoreBearerAuthenticator : BearerAuthenticator`). It is therefore an instance of BearerAuthenticator and inherits the redacted representation under its own runtime class name, for example `PetStoreBearerAuthenticator(host=..., token=***)`.
- java: BearerAuthenticator, BasicAuthenticator and ApiKeyAuthenticator are `final`, so the wrapper extends BaseAuthenticator and delegates to a private BearerAuthenticator. `instanceof BearerAuthenticator` is false, and toString falls back to `PetStoreBearerAuthenticator@1b6d3586`.
- rust: the wrapper is a tuple struct `pub struct PetStoreBearerAuthenticator(BearerAuthenticator)` with no Debug impl (and no derive). It cannot be `{:?}`-formatted, against Rust API guideline C-DEBUG and unlike every other rust authenticator, which has a hand-written redacting Debug.
- go and node: the base String() / inspect hard-code "BearerAuthenticator{...}" / "BearerAuthenticator(...)", so the wrapper prints the base class name instead of its own.
None of this is forced: java's generic authenticators need not be final, rust can delegate Debug to self.0, and go and node can use the runtime type name.

## F401 [low] Per-scheme authenticators cannot be imported from the node or dart package; only java and kotlin test them
- Status: **open** | Lens: L21-api-surface | Category: api-shape | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: node, dart, python, csharp, php, ruby, go, rust, swift, elixir

Every SDK generates per-scheme authenticator classes (PetStoreBearerAuthenticator, AdminBasicAuthenticator, ApiKeyHeaderAuthenticator, SessionCookieAuthenticator, MachineAuthClientCredentialsAuthenticator, and others). They are public and importable in java, kotlin, csharp, php, ruby, go, rust (`pub use` in auth/mod.rs), swift and elixir. node's package.json `exports` only has ".", and src/index.ts re-exports only the generic Basic, Bearer and ApiKey authenticators plus OAuth2*. All 11 node per-scheme classes, plus BaseAuthenticator, OAuth2TokenManager and the ApiHttpResponse type (which the exported ApiClient interface returns), are therefore unreachable to consumers. dart's barrel exports base_authenticator and oauth2_token_manager but no per-scheme file, so using one needs a `package:.../src/` import, which the dart analyzer flags. python's `auth/__init__.py` does not re-export them either (they can still be imported by full module path). Coverage differs too: only java and kotlin PetApiTest use PetStoreBearerAuthenticator and AdminBasicAuthenticator, and the other 10 have no test of any per-scheme wrapper. Either export them uniformly with a test in each SDK, or stop generating them where they are unreachable.

The result-returning variant is `addPetWithHttpInfo` or `add_pet_with_http_info` in java, kotlin, php, node, python, ruby, rust and elixir, and `AddPetWithHttpInfoAsync` in csharp. go and swift use `WithHTTPInfo`, which is idiomatic there: Go initialisms and the Swift API guidelines' uniform acronym case. dart emits `addPetWithHTTPInfo` for every operation. ## F403 [low] dart's barrel exports the no-auth sentinel (`noAuth`, `NoAuthAuthenticator`) as public API; the other SDKs hide it
- Status: **fixed** | Lens: L21-api-surface | Category: api-shape | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False
- SDKs: dart

The NO_AUTH sentinel is meant to be internal: operations declared `security: []` pass it to suppress the client authenticator. python's docstring says it "never leaves the generated client; callers never see it", and ruby, php and elixir say the same. It is hidden in kotlin (`internal object NoAuth`), csharp (`internal sealed class NoAuth`), java (`protected static` in BaseApi), go (unexported), rust (`pub(crate)`), swift (internal) and node (not re-exported from the package root), and elixir marks it `@doc false`. dart declares `class NoAuthAuthenticator` and `const Authenticator noAuth` in src/auth/authenticator.dart, and the package barrel exports that file without `hide`. Dart consumers therefore get `noAuth` as a documented public symbol they can pass as a per-call `auth` to strip credentials from any operation, which no other strongly-encapsulating SDK allows. The fix is `export 'src/auth/authenticator.dart' hide noAuth, NoAuthAuthenticator;` or a library-private name. (php's public `Auth\NoAuth` and python's and ruby's public names come from those languages' lack of package-private visibility, though `@internal`, a leading underscore and `private_constant` are available.)
- `src/spec/resources/generated/dart/lib/petstore_client.dart:20` — export 'src/auth/authenticator.dart';
- `src/spec/resources/generated/dart/lib/src/auth/authenticator.dart:71` — const Authenticator noAuth = NoAuthAuthenticator._();
- `src/spec/resources/generated/kotlin/src/main/kotlin/com/example/petstore/auth/Authenticator.kt:64` — internal object NoAuth : Authenticator {
- `src/spec/resources/generated/csharp/src/PetstoreClient/Auth/IAuthenticator.cs:74` — internal sealed class NoAuth : IAuthenticator
- `src/spec/resources/generated/python/petstore_client/api/base_api.py:44` — never leaves the generated client; callers never see it.

## F405 [low] Only php's Client facade accepts an injected transport (plus a php-only Psr18ApiClient); the other 11 hard-wire a private DefaultApiClient per Client
- Status: **open** | Lens: L22-lifecycle | Category: api-shape | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: php, java, kotlin, csharp, python, ruby, node, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir

php's Client::__construct, withToken and withAuthenticator take `?ApiClient $apiClient` and ship a Psr18ApiClient adapter, so a php caller can share one transport and connection pool across several Client instances or bring a framework-managed client. In the other 11 the facade always does `new DefaultApiClient(transportOptions)` internally (dart even through a private constructor). A caller cannot share a pool between Clients or plug in a custom ApiClient through the facade, even though every SDK defines a public ApiClient interface. Combined with the documented T2-11 (the facades are not closeable), every Client built in those 11 SDKs owns a pool the caller can neither reuse nor release. The PSR-18 adapter is idiomatic php, but a facade-level transport parameter is not php-specific.

- `src/spec/resources/generated/php/lib/Client.php:76` — $apiClient ??= new DefaultApiClient($transportOptions);

- `src/spec/resources/generated/dart/lib/src/client.dart:68` — final apiClient = DefaultApiClient(transportOptions: transportOptions);

## F406 [low] SDKs disagree on whether they close a caller-supplied upload stream or file handle
- Status: **open** | Lens: L22-lifecycle | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: go, java, python, ruby, php, csharp

python (_multipart_part closes any .read()-able value), ruby (multipart_part ensure value.close), php (fclose on resource parts) and csharp (StreamContent disposed with the HttpRequestMessage) close a stream the caller passed in. go never closes an *os.File or io.Reader part, and even Seek(0)s the file first, which changes what is read compared with the others, which read from the current position. java closes an InputStream multipart part (try (stream)) but leaves a raw-body InputStream open (stream.readAllBytes() with no close). The same upload therefore leaves the handle open or closed depending on the language, and reuses or rewinds it differently.

Reviewer suspected this is forced: Go convention is that the caller owns io.Closer, but python's requests-style convention is the same, so the choice is not forced either way.

## F407 [low] Timeout budget across a redirect chain: whole chain in go/node/swift, per hop in the other 9
- Status: **open** | Lens: L22-lifecycle | Category: behavior | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): True
- SDKs: go, node, swift, java, kotlin, csharp, python, ruby, php, rust, dart, elixir

The same `timeout` gives different total budgets once redirects are followed. go's http.Client.Timeout covers the whole Do() including redirects. node builds one AbortSignal.timeout and spreads it into every redirect fetch. swift's timeoutIntervalForResource covers the whole URLSessionTask including delegate-followed redirects. java (redirectBuilder.timeout per hop), kotlin (per request), csharp (HttpClient.Timeout per SendAsync), python (urllib3 Timeout per request), ruby, php (max_duration per request), rust (per send) and elixir (a new Task per recursive hop) re-arm the deadline on every hop. With timeout=5s and up to 20 redirects, a call fails at about 5s in go/node/swift but can run about 105s elsewhere.

Reviewer suspected this is forced: go's Client.Timeout and swift's resource timeout are whole-transfer by library design. Either side could be made to match: per-hop with a per-request ctx/timeout in go and node, or a total budget in the manual-loop languages.
- `src/spec/resources/generated/go/pkg/default_api_client.go:299` — client.Timeout = time.Duration(*opts.Timeout()) * time.Millisecond

- `src/spec/resources/generated/java/src/main/java/com/example/petstore/DefaultApiClient.java:541` — redirectBuilder.timeout(Duration.ofMillis(transportOptions.getTimeout()));
- `src/spec/resources/generated/elixir/lib/petstore_client/default_api_client.ex:797` — task = Task.async(req_fun)

## F408 [low] Unsynchronized mutable auth state in the implicit and authorization-code authenticators (java/go/swift/csharp); kotlin uses @Volatile and rust a Mutex

OAuth2ImplicitAuthenticator.accessToken and OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator.tokenExchanged are written by setAccessToken/exchangeCode (typically on a callback thread) and read by getAuthHeaders on request threads. kotlin marks both @Volatile and rust wraps both in Mutex. java uses plain fields, which gives no happens-before, so a request thread can keep seeing null or false. go uses plain fields, a data race that `go test -race` flags and a torn read of a string header. swift's classes declare @unchecked Sendable over plain `var accessToken: String` and `var tokenExchanged: Bool`, a data race on a refcounted String. csharp uses plain fields. dart, node, php, ruby, python and elixir are not exposed: single-threaded, GIL-protected or immutable.

## F411 [low] rust DefaultApiClient::close() only sets a flag and releases nothing, despite its docs
- Status: **open** (template/README text, not a rule document: still open) | Lens: L22-lifecycle | Category: doc-truth | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): False
- SDKs: rust

The trait impl documents close() as 'Releases the underlying transport'. It only stores closed=true. The reqwest::Client, with its pool, idle sockets and hyper connections, lives until the last Arc<dyn ApiClient> is dropped. The Client facade, every *Api and every HTTP-aware authenticator hold clones, so in practice it lives until all of them are dropped. java (HttpClient.close), go (CloseIdleConnections), python (pool clear), csharp (Dispose), kotlin (HttpClient.close), node (dispatcher.close), dart (client.close), swift (finishTasksAndInvalidate) and php (reset) do release their pools on close. elixir documents that its pool is global, and ruby has no pool (see the pooling finding). rust can hold Mutex<Option<reqwest::Client>> and take() it on close.
- `src/spec/resources/generated/rust/src/default_api_client.rs:82` — pub fn close(&self) { self.closed.store(true, Ordering::SeqCst); }
- `src/spec/resources/generated/rust/src/default_api_client.rs:102` — /// Releases the underlying transport.
- `src/spec/resources/generated/go/pkg/default_api_client.go:267` — transport.CloseIdleConnections()

## F655 [medium] The expanded spec broke the go golden in seven ways, each fixed in this commit: tag, operation and parameter descriptions with newlines broke // comments (new goLineComment lambda); the server descrip
- Status: **open** (reported by the go fix agent, unverified) | Lens: batch5-discovered | Category: discovered | Unit-testable (reviewer's view): None
- SDKs: go

The expanded spec broke the go golden in seven ways, each fixed in this commit: tag, operation and parameter descriptions with newlines broke // comments (new goLineComment lambda); the server description and variables were not escaped as Go strings or comments (new goStringLiteral and goBlockComment lambdas); server enum constants came out as A&amp;B and IT&#39;S (new goIdentPart lambda plus triple-brace values); the Mirror and Regional variants both declared GetMultiServerPetInfoServerRegion (enum types are now qualified by variant name, which renames the existing public server enum types); the 2ndPage option and the 2fa field were not legal exported identifiers (N prefix: N2ndPage, N2fa); the Swatch enum-ref default was emitted as Swatch.Green (now SwatchGreen); the ' ' enum value produced a constant named Separator, the same as its type (now the empty-value name); EdgeCases referenced Error while the type is declared ModelError (getTypeDeclaration resolves refs through toModelName).
